podcast.body: This song reached number one on Billboard's Hot 100 for eight consecutive weeks, making it 1983's Top Hit and surpassing Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean." Sting wrote it about a stalker, though many listeners perceived it as an impassioned love song. By 2019, BMI recognized it as the most played song in radio history, largely due to Andy Summers' guitar arpeggio and Stuart Copeland's cracking snare drum rhythm. Its acclaimed music video featured the band depicted as jazzmen, bathed in shadow, in black and white. "every breath you take reached number one on Billboard's Hot 100, a song that its writer Sting called Evil and Sinister, spent eight weeks on top making it 1983's Top Hit."

podcast.body: This song spent eight weeks at number one and is often mistaken for a love song, but songwriter Sting himself described it as "a fairly nasty song about surveillance and ownership and jealousy." It was an omnipresent, irresistible, and unavoidable hit, remarkably surpassing the success of Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" in a year flooded with "Thriller" hits. Fourteen years later, it spawned Puff Daddy's chart-topping homage to Biggie Smalls, "I'll Be Missing You." "Sting himself has called it, quote, a fairly nasty song about surveillance and ownership and jealousy."

podcast.body: This song was The Police's biggest hit, though it was "not as romantic as it seemed," being about control and obsession. Its melody was interpolated by Puff Daddy for his massive 1997 hit "I'll Be Missing You." In 2007, a lawsuit regarding the song's publishing was making its way through the legal system. "Although the band's biggest hit, every breath you take, was not as romantic as it seemed."

podcast.body: This song was the ubiquitous winner of the 1983 Billboard Song of the Summer. It is described as the "sultriest hit Sting ever wrote," originally an "ode to stalking and surveillance" that the public largely "mistook for a love song." The track's sound, characterized by Sting's moody bass line and Andy Summers' crackling guitar, is said to evoke a hot summer night. It holds the distinction of being the only Song of the Summer to be sampled in another year's Song of the Summer. "Even if it had had no lyrics, the police's biggest hit would sound like a hot summer night between Sting's moody bass line and Andy Summers crackling guitar."
